articles.title: Crescent Biopharma Announces FDA Clearance of IND Application for CR-002, a PD-L1-targeted Topoisomerase Inhibitor ADC, for the Treatment of Solid Tumors
articles.text:
Accessibility: Skip TopNav Crescent Biopharma Announces Grants of Inducement Awards October 06, 2026 16:15 ET | Source: Crescent Biopharma, Inc. Crescent Biopharma, Inc. WALTHAM, Mass., Oct.  06, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Crescent Biopharma , Inc. (“Crescent” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: CBIO), a clinical-stage biotechnology company dedicated to rapidly advancing the next wave of therapies for cancer patients, today announced that the independent Compensation Committee of its Board of Directors approved the grant of options to purchase an aggregate of 81,525 shares of the Company’s ordinary shares to six non-executive employees as equity inducement awards under the Crescent Biopharma, Inc. 2025 Employment Inducement Incentive Award Plan, as amended (the “Inducement Plan”). The options were approved on October 5, 2026 and were material to each employee's acceptance of employment with Crescent, in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4). The options were granted with a 10-year term and an exercise price equal to $13.94, the closing price per share of Crescent’s ordinary shares as reported by Nasdaq on October 5, 2026. The options granted to each employee shall vest and become exercisable as to one-fourth (1/4th) of the shares subject to the respective options on the first anniversary of the employee’s start date, and one-forty-eighth (1/48th) of the shares subject to the respective options shall vest and become exercisable monthly thereafter, in each case, subject to continuous service with Crescent through the applicable vesting dates. The options are subject to the terms of the Inducement Plan and the terms and conditions of an option agreement covering the applicable grant. About Crescent Biopharma Crescent Biopharma’s vision is to build a world leading oncology company bringing the next wave of therapies for cancer patients. The Company’s clinical-stage pipeline includes its lead program, a PD-1 x VEGF bispecific antibody, as well as novel antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs). By leveraging multiple modalities and established targets, Crescent aims to rapidly advance potentially transformative therapies as single agents and as part of combination regimens to treat a range of solid tumors. For more information, visit www.crescentbiopharma.com and follow the Company on LinkedIn and X . The China In Vitro Fertilization Market is projected to grow from US$ 5.05 billion in 2025 to US$ 15.29 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 13.1% from 2026 to 2034. Market expansion is being supported by rising infertility rates, delayed parenthood, favorable demographic policies, increasing acceptance of assisted reproductive technologies, and continued investment in fertility clinics and advanced reproductive care. China In Vitro Fertilization Market Overview Demand for IVF treatment in China is increasing as lifestyle changes, work-related stress, pollution, late marriage, and delayed childbearing affect reproductive health. The transition from the one-child policy to policies encouraging second and third births has also strengthened interest in fertility services. Specialized reproductive hospitals and private fertility clinics are expanding their capabilities through genetic screening, frozen embryo transfer, time-lapse embryo monitoring, cryopreservation, and artificial intelligence-based embryo assessment. Insurance coverage for infertility treatment is also emerging in selected regions, helping improve affordability and access for some patients. Greater awareness and cultural acceptance of assisted reproduction are expected to support sustained China IVF market growth. Key China IVF Market Growth Drivers Rising Infertility Rates and Delayed Parenthood Infertility is becoming more prevalent among men and women in China. Urbanization, smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyles, environmental exposure, hormonal imbalances, and demanding work schedules are contributing to reproductive health challenges. At the same time, more couples are postponing parenthood because of education, career development, financial planning, and changing social priorities. Age-related fertility decline and increasing male infertility are driving more patients toward IVF services. In response, healthcare providers are expanding fertility programs, recruiting reproductive specialists, and investing in modern laboratory systems to manage growing patient volumes. Supportive Government Policies and Fertility Initiatives China's demographic policies are creating a more favorable environment for fertility treatment. Government encouragement of larger families has increased public discussion of reproductive health and improved the acceptance of assisted reproductive services. Selected regional authorities have started including certain infertility treatments in medical insurance programs, reducing part of the financial burden on eligible families. Policy support is also encouraging investment in reproductive medicine, clinical infrastructure, professional training, and fertility research. Greater regulatory clarity and broader access initiatives could further increase patient confidence and strengthen the long-term outlook for the China In Vitro Fertilization Market. Reproductive Technology and Clinical Innovation Chinese fertility centers are adopting preimplantation genetic testing (PGT), time-lapse embryo imaging, advanced cryopreservation, minimally invasive techniques, laboratory automation, and artificial intelligence-based embryo selection. These technologies can improve clinical decision-making, laboratory efficiency, treatment safety, and patient outcomes. Partnerships with international reproductive technology companies are helping clinics gain access to advanced equipment and next-generation fertility solutions. Continued digitalization is also improving patient management, laboratory workflows, and treatment monitoring. China IVF Market Challenges High Treatment Costs and Limited Insurance Coverage IVF treatment remains costly because of medication expenses, laboratory requirements, advanced equipment, and specialist expertise. Patients may require multiple cycles, increasing total out-of-pocket spending. Although selected regions have expanded insurance support, coverage remains uneven and many households continue to face affordability barriers. Regional Differences in Access to Fertility Care Advanced IVF centers are concentrated in major metropolitan areas, while rural and less-developed regions often have fewer specialized facilities and trained professionals. Patients outside large cities may need to travel significant distances, adding costs and disrupting treatment continuity. High demand can also lead to extended waiting times at leading hospitals. Expanding fertility infrastructure and specialist training will be essential to improving nationwide access. Major City Market Insights Shanghai In Vitro Fertilization Market Shanghai benefits from advanced healthcare infrastructure, experienced fertility specialists, modern laboratories, and a high-income population. Delayed childbirth among working professionals is contributing to demand, while the city attracts patients from surrounding provinces seeking specialized reproductive care. Investment in clinical technology and government efforts to support childbirth are expected to reinforce Shanghai's position as a major IVF market. Beijing In Vitro Fertilization Market Beijing is a leading center for reproductive medicine, supported by prominent research institutions, established fertility hospitals, and advanced clinical expertise. Clinics offer services including PGT, cryopreservation, and AI-assisted embryo assessment. Strong medical research capabilities and demand from patients across northern China continue to support market development. Shenzhen In Vitro Fertilization Market Shenzhen's IVF market is expanding alongside its private healthcare sector and technology-focused medical ecosystem. Fertility providers are integrating digital health platforms, AI-powered diagnostic tools, and laboratory automation. Delayed parenthood, intense work schedules, and rising demand from the Greater Bay Area are creating opportunities for premium and technology-enabled reproductive services. The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said. “The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. Perspective Back to Top Krish Patel, MD Krish Patel, MD For more than 2 decades, R-CHOP has been the global standard of care for newly diagnosed patients with DLBCL, leading to cure in about 60% of patients. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. Krish Patel, MD SCRI Oncology Partners Sarah Cannon Research Institute Disclosures: Patel reports research funding to his institution from, consulting/advisory roles with or speakers bureau roles with AbbVie, AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Genentech, Genmab, Janssen, Kite Pharma, Merck, Pfizer, Sanofi and other companies. Perspective Back to Top Tycel Phillips, MD Tycel Phillips, MD Improving response and curability remains paramount for management of patients with first-line DLBCL, despite improvement of salvage options. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Tycel Phillips, MD City of Hope Disclosures: Phillips reports research support from, advisory board roles with or scientific board roles with AbbVie, Adaptive, ADC Therapeutics, AstraZeneca, BeOne Medicines, Bristol Myers Squibb, Caribou, Eli Lilly & Co., Epizyme, Genentech, Genmab, Gilead Sciences, Incyte, Janssen/Johnson & Johnson, Kite Pharma, Legend Biotech, Merck, Pfizer, Pharmacyclics, Seagen and Sobi. The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Key takeaways:
The addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to first-line R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% for patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The regimen could become a standard in this setting.
The addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to first-line R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% for patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas.
The regimen could become a standard in this setting.
CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial.
Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD
Krish Patel, MD;
Tycel Phillips, MD
The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed.
diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago.
The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting.
Georg Lenz
“I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.”
Georg Lenz, MD
An unmet need
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases.
R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades.
However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease.
“We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said.
Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant.
The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL.
Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas.
The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL.
All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment.
Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles.
PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints.
‘Good chance’ for cure
Median follow-up reached 35.2 months.
The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed.
The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin.
Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%).
“Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.”
Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%).
An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival.
“We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said.
‘Manageable’ toxicities
The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events.
Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%).
More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%).
Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles.
“The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.”
Evolving treatment landscape
The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment.
The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting.
The New England Journal of Medicine
Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment.
The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL.
epcoritamab
The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said.
“The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out.
“Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.”

Perspective Back to Top Krish Patel, MD Krish Patel, MD For more than 2 decades, R-CHOP has been the global standard of care for newly diagnosed patients with DLBCL, leading to cure in about 60% of patients. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. Perspective Back to Top Tycel Phillips, MD Tycel Phillips, MD Improving response and curability remains paramount for management of patients with first-line DLBCL, despite improvement of salvage options. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. articles.title: 15 biotech companies in China you should know about
articles.text:
Skip to content Suggested Topics: Home Best in Biotech 15 biotech companies in China you should know about Photo credits: Hanson Lu Add Labiotech as your Google Preferred Source Newsletter Signup - Under Article / In Page " * " indicates required fields China’s biotech scene has evolved significantly over the last few years, with companies increasingly developing novel drugs and attracting international attention through partnerships and out-licensing deals. Earlier this week, the country set out its latest five-year plan for its pharma industry, with an aim of being responsible for at least 25% of first-in-class drugs on the global market in order to cement its emerging status as a hotbed for innovative research and development (R&D). In this article, we look at 15 Chinese companies that are currently contributing to the country’s thriving biotech industry. Table of contents Abogen Biosciences Technology: mRNA therapies Disease areas: Oncology, immunology, and infectious diseases Recent news: Initiated phase 3 trial of shingles vaccine candidate ABO1108 Abogen Biosciences makes it onto this list by virtue of an impressive $700 million series C round that it bagged in August 2021 – still one of the biggest ever private biotech funding rounds. This was swiftly followed by another $300 million investment round in November 2021. Abogen is one of the few Chinese biotech companies that has self-developed all its key messenger RNA (mRNA) platform technologies, across mRNA synthesis, delivery, and manufacturing. Its mission is ultimately to develop therapies derived from mRNA technology , including immunotherapies for cancer, protein replacement therapies, and vaccines for infectious diseases, including a vaccine against COVID-19, which was granted emergency use authorization (EUA) in Indonesia in 2022, making it the first China-made mRNA vaccine authorized for use anywhere in the world. The mRNA company’s lead candidate is ABO2011, which is currently being tested in a phase 1/2 trial as a monotherapy or in combination with the monoclonal antibody drug toripalimab in patients with advanced solid tumors. Another of its main candidates, a shingles vaccine dubbed ABO1108, which trains the immune system to fight the varicella-zoster virus, entered into a phase 3 trial in June 2026. Also part of Abogen’s portfolio is a novel KRAS mRNA cancer vaccine, ABO2102, in both China and the U.S. According to the company, the candidate is China’s first therapeutic cancer vaccine targeting multiple – in this case five – KRAS mutations. Antengene Technology: T cell engagers and antibody therapies Disease areas: Oncology and immunology Recent news:  Entered into a partnership with K2 Therapeutics for ATG-106 Antengene is focused primarily on developing therapies for oncology and immunology indications. The Chinese biotech company’s pipeline spans from preclinical to commercial, with key investigational candidates including the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) ATG-022, the oral CD73 inhibitor ATG-037, the bispecific antibody ATG-101, the bispecific ADC ATG-125, the bifunctional fusion protein ATG-207, as well as T cell engager programs developed using Antengene’s proprietary AnTenGager platform. The first patient was dosed in a phase 3 trial of ATG-022 earlier this week. To date, Antengene has obtained 33 investigational new drug approvals in the U.S. and Asia, and obtained new drug application approvals in 10 Asia-Pacific markets. Its lead commercial asset, XPOVIO (selinexor), is approved in mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, South Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Australia, and has been included in the national insurance schemes in five of these markets. Suggested Articles Is China the future of biotech? Genetic engineering giants: is China poised to lead the way? 10 biotech companies leading innovation in the Asia-Pacific region Seven companies leading the mRNA revolution in biotechnology Eight biotech companies spearheading the antibody drug conjugate new wave Over the past year, the company has formed several key deals. In March, the Chinese biotech company entered into a global license agreement with UCB, granting the Belgian biopharma worldwide exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize its asset ATG-201, a CD19/CD3 bispecific T-cell engager (TCE) antibody targeting B cell-related autoimmune diseases. A few months later, Antengene also announced an exclusive license agreement with K2 Therapeutics for ATG-106, a preclinical CDH6 x CD3 bispecific T cell engager in development for solid tumors, as well as an option agreement to grant K2 Therapeutics the option to obtain exclusive global rights to develop and commercialize an undisclosed preclinical bispecific T cell engager candidate. Argo Biopharma Technology: siRNA therapies Disease areas: Cardiovascular diseases, rare diseases , and viral infections. Recent news: Dosed first patient in phase 1 trial of BW-41012 for the prevention of thromboembolic diseases Argo Biopharma is working on the development of next-generation siRNA therapies and has established a pipeline of drug candidates targeting a wide range of indications, including cardiovascular diseases, rare diseases, viral infections, and metabolic diseases, with eight therapeutic candidates currently in clinical development, according to its website. To help create its candidates, the company utilizes an siRNA drug discovery engine, called RADS (RNA molecules with superior Activity, Durability, and Safety), which aims to produce more stable, long-acting siRNA molecules. In September 2025, the Chinese biotech company announced that it had entered into an additional strategic collaboration with Novartis for multiple cardiovascular assets in Argo’s pipeline. More specifically, the deal allowed Novartis to explore Argo’s phase 2 asset BW-00112 (ANGPTL3) in a combination study for dyslipidemia, and the Swiss giant also has the first right of negotiation to secure the license to the candidate further down the line. This agreement expanded the companies’ existing partnership, as they originally collaborated in January 2024 for multiple programs. Most recently, in July, Argo announced that it had dosed the first patient in a phase 1 trial of BW-41012, an investigational siRNA therapy targeting factor XI (FXI) for the prevention of thromboembolic diseases. DualityBio Technology: ADCs Disease areas: Oncology and immunology Recent news: Entered into a partnership with Genentech to develop next-generation ADCs Dedicated to developing next-generation ADCs for patients with cancer and autoimmune diseases, DualityBio has built multiple next-generation ADC technology platforms with global intellectual property rights and has established a robust clinical-stage ADC pipeline, for which it is conducting multiple global clinical trials across nearly 20 countries, with over 3,500 patients enrolled to date. The company’s most advanced candidate is the topoisomerase-1 inhibitor-based ADC DB-1303 (also known as trastuzumab pamirtecan or BNT323), which is being developed in collaboration with BioNTech after the two companies agreed to a partnership deal in 2023 in which BioNTech received exclusive licenses from DualityBio for two investigational ADC assets (DB-1303 and DB-1311) directed against targets expressed in a broad range of human cancers. In September last year, the companies announced that a phase 3 trial of DB-1303 conducted in China met its primary endpoint of progression-free survival at a pre-specified interim analysis in patients with HER2-positive unresectable or metastatic breast cancer who have previously received trastuzumab and a taxane-based chemotherapy. At the time of the announcement, DualityBio said that it planned to begin the process for potential regulatory submission in China. Subsequently, in April 2026, the Chinese biotech company announced that the Biologics License Application for the asset had been accepted for review by the China National Medical Products Administration (NMPA). BioNTech is not the only company that DualityBio has struck an important partnership with; its latest deal , made in August, was with Roche’s Genentech to develop next-generation ADCs built on DualityBio’s DUPAC novel-payload platform. DUPAC is one of the company’s four ADC technology platforms and comprises multiple payloads with novel mechanisms of action designed to address resistance to the payload classes underlying currently approved ADCs. Epigenic Therapeutics Technology: Gene modulation therapy Disease areas: Metabolic and liver diseases, ophthalmology, CNS disorders, and immuno-oncology Recent news: Was given IND clearance by the NMPA to study EPI-003 in the clinic in mainland China Epigenic Therapeutics is dedicated to developing next-generation gene modulation therapy utilizing epigenome regulation to treat prevalent diseases. The company has multiple product candidates in the pipeline, spanning disease areas such as metabolic and liver diseases, ophthalmology, central nervous system (CNS) disorders, and immuno-oncology. Epigenic’s technology platform, called EPIREG, enables efficient, durable, and specific silencing of target genes through precise DNA methylation and histone modification. According to the company, unlike traditional gene-editing tools that rely on DNA cleavage, its platform offers a “safer and revolutionary therapeutic approach” for patients with chronic diseases, effectively mitigating safety concerns associated with conventional gene editing. The Chinese biotech company’s most advanced candidate is EPI-003, which is being developed as a functional cure for hepatitis B; the candidate was already in phase 1 trials across New Zealand, Australia, and Hong Kong, before the company announced in January that it had also been given investigational new drug (IND) clearance by the NMPA to be studied in the clinic in mainland China. This is significant as China carries one of the highest burdens of hepatitis B globally, accounting for one-third of the world’s chronic hepatitis B cases. In September 2025, Epigenic announced that it had completed a $60 million series B round, which it said would primarily support the ongoing clinical development of EPI-003, as well as the development of one of the company’s other candidates, EPI-001, for hypercholesterolemia (high cholesterol). The company said the funding will also accelerate the advancement of multiple preclinical programs and further strengthen its technology platforms. Everest Medicines Technology: mRNA therapies and others Disease areas: Immunology, ophthalmology, critical care, and CKM (cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic) diseases Recent news: Entered into a licensing agreement with Dimerix for the development and commercialization of DMX-200 Everest Medicines is focused on discovering, developing, manufacturing, and commercializing innovative therapies that address critical unmet medical needs for patients in global markets. Its disease areas of focus include autoimmune, ophthalmology, critical care, and CKM (cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic) diseases, and it is leveraging its mRNA platform to advance its existing pipeline, including mRNA in vivo CAR-T and mRNA cancer vaccines, while selectively expanding into additional high-value therapeutic areas with blockbuster potential and accelerating its global expansion. The Chinese biotech company already has four approved commercial products: NEFECON, a corticosteroid for primary IgA nephropathy in adults at risk of disease progression; VELSIPITY, a selective sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator for adult patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis; XERAVA, a fluorocycline intravenous antibiotic for complicated intra-abdominal infections in adult patients; and CARDAMYST, a rapid-acting calcium channel blocker nasal spray for adults with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (a type of abnormal heart rhythm). Everest Medicines has entered multiple partnerships over the summer. In June alone, it announced three separate deals: one with Travere Therapeutics for the development and commercialization of civorebrutinib (also known as EVER001), a covalent reversible Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor for patients with rare, immune-mediated kidney diseases, in all markets outside China and certain countries in East and Southeast Asia; one with LENZ Therapeutics, in which Everest Medicines acquired rights to develop and commercialize VIZZ (LNZ100), an aceclidine-based eye drop for the treatment of presbyopia (the gradual loss of your eyes’ ability to focus on nearby objects), in Greater China; and one with Dimerix for the development and commercialization of DMX-200, a small molecule inhibitor of the chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) for the treatment of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (a type of glomerular disease that involves scarring in your kidney), in Greater China, South Korea, and certain Southeast Asian countries. Hangzhou DAC Biotech Technology: ADCs Disease area: Oncology Recent news: Unveiled phase 1 data for DXC006 showing the candidate’s promise in SCLC Also known as Hangzhou Duoxi Bio, Hangzhou DAC Biotech is developing proprietary ADCs for treating cancer . After many years of R&D, Hangzhou DAC has established a special ADC technology platform, with 18 ADC drugs in different development stages currently listed in its pipeline, ultimately making the company a leader in the field in China. The company’s current lead clinical candidate is a CD56-targeted ADC called DXC006 for the treatment of solid tumors, including small cell lung cancer (SCLC), NSCLC, and neuroendocrine carcinoma. In June 2026, phase 1 data was unveiled at ASCO demonstrating the candidate’s promise in SCLC. Among second-line SCLC patients, DXC006 monotherapy achieved an objective response rate (ORR) of 75% and a disease control rate (DCR) of 100%. Meanwhile, in heavily pretreated later-line SCLC patients, the ORR was 59.3%, and the DCR was 89.8%. In 2024, the Chinese biotech company entered into a license and collaboration agreement with WuXi Biologics and Aadi Bioscience, in which Aadi was granted the exclusive global rights to develop and commercialize three preclinical ADCs from Hangzhou DAC and WuXi Bio. Furthermore, back in 2022, Hangzhou DAC announced a collaboration and license agreement with Janssen for the development of novel ADCs. Under the terms of the collaboration, it was agreed that Hangzhou DAC would apply its ADC platform to Janssen’s proprietary antibodies, with the aim of developing novel ADC products against up to five targets. Harbour BioMed Technology: Antibody therapies Disease areas: Immunology and oncology Recent news: Announced that its partner, Windward Bio, initiated a phase 3 trial of HBM9378/WIN378 in patients with asthma Committed to the discovery and development of novel antibody therapeutics in immunology and oncology, Harbour BioMed is building a robust and differentiated pipeline through internal R&D capabilities, strategic global collaborations in co-discovery and co-development, and selective acquisitions. Harbour BioMed also has its own proprietary antibody technology platform, Harbour Mice, which generates fully human monoclonal antibodies in both the conventional two heavy and two light chain (H2L2) format and the heavy chain-only (HCAb) format. Building upon HCAb antibodies, the company says that its HCAb-based immune cell engagers bispecific antibody technology enables tumor-killing effects that traditional combination therapies cannot achieve. Additionally, the HCAb-based bispecific immune cell antagonist technology empowers the development of innovative biologics for immunological and inflammatory diseases. Earlier this month, the company announced that its partner , Windward Bio, reported positive interim results from a phase 2 trial of the candidate HBM9378/WIN378, an ultra-long-acting monoclonal antibody with a unique binding mode to inhibit thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) for the treatment of asthma. The first phase 3 study has now been initiated, while a second phase 3 trial is planned to begin in the first half of 2027. In June last year, Harbour BioMed entered into a strategic collaboration with Japanese pharma giant Otsuka to advance BCMAxCD3 bispecific T-cell engagers for the treatment of autoimmune diseases. Furthermore, in March 2025, the Chinese biotech company also announced a strategic collaboration with AstraZeneca to discover and develop next-generation multi-specific antibodies for immunology, oncology, and beyond. The deal included an option to license multiple programs utilizing Harbour BioMed’s technology platform in multiple therapeutic areas, as well as a $105 million equity investment by AstraZeneca in Harbour BioMed. HUTCHMED Technology: Antibody therapies and others Disease area: Oncology Recent news: Announced an exclusive development and license agreement with a subsidiary of GSK for HMPL-A830 HUTCHMED was among the first global-focused novel drug discovery companies in China and, over the past two decades, it has established a fully integrated R&D platform with world-class discovery and development capabilities. Its focus is to bring cancer drug candidates from in-house discovery to patients around the world, with four medicines currently marketed in China; one of these (fruquintinib) is also approved around the world, including in the U.S., Europe, and Japan, marketed by its partner Takeda. The company has also developed a profitable commercial platform with deep pan-China market access, which manufactures, markets, and distributes its novel oncology products, as well as prescription drugs and consumer health products in China. HUTCHMED has forged several partnerships over the years, including with big pharma companies AstraZeneca, Eli Lilly, and Takeda. Its most recent deal came at the beginning of this month, as it announced an exclusive development and license agreement with a subsidiary of GSK, granting the GSK subsidiary worldwide rights – excluding mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan – to develop and commercialize HMPL-A830, a first-in-class KRAS-EGFR antibody-targeted therapy conjugate that is expected to enter clinical trials in H2 2026. Innogen Technology: GLP-1 therapies Disease area: Metabolic disorders Recent news: Received approval from NMPA in China for its lead asset Efsubaglutide Alfa Founded in 2014, Innogen is dedicated to the research and development of innovative and affordable medicines for diabetes and other metabolic disease patients. In late 2021, the firm raised $120 million in venture financing , which helped it advance its fusion protein drug, Efsubaglutide Alfa, into phase 3 trials. The drug eventually received approval from the NMPA in 2025 for blood glucose control in adult patients with type 2 diabetes. The drug is designed to activate glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). Now a very well-known target for the treatment of metabolic disorders, GLP-1 promotes the secretion of insulin, a hormone vital for stopping blood sugar levels from getting too high. Insulin is either scarce or doesn’t work well in patients with type 2 diabetes. While there are a number of GLP-1 agonists on the market, such as Wegovy and Ozempic, efsubaglutide alfa is designed to last longer in the body than some of its competitors. Efsubaglutide alfa is also under development by Innogen for other indications, such as obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), to address the large unmet therapeutic needs in these disease areas. Innovent Biologics Technology: ADCs Disease areas: Oncology, cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, immunology, and ophthalmology Recent news: Entered into an exclusive agreement with Daiichi Sankyo in August for the commercialization of Vanflyta (quizartinib) in China Founded in 2011 with the mission to empower patients worldwide with affordable, high-quality therapies, Innovent discovers, develops, manufactures, and commercializes innovative medicines that target cancer, cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, autoimmune diseases, and eye diseases. Innovent has already launched 20 products in the market and has one asset under NMPA review, five assets in phase 3 or pivotal clinical trials, and 14 more molecules in early clinical stage. The company’s lead investigational asset is arcotatug tavatecan (IBI343), which in June became the world’s first CLDN18.2 ADC to be submitted for regulatory review after it met its primary endpoint in a phase 3 trial for the treatment of advanced gastric cancer and its new drug application was accepted by the NMPA. The therapy is designed to selectively deliver a high-potency exatecan payload (TOPO1i) to tumor cells via a cleavable linker, and incorporates Fc silencing to minimize off-tumor toxicities. Innovent has entered into several partnerships with big pharma companies over the past year, including a license and collaboration agreement with Takeda in October 2025 for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of two of Innovent’s late-stage oncology medicines, a licensing and collaboration agreement with Pfizer in May 2026 for the research and development of 12 promising new breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines, and an exclusive agreement with Daiichi Sankyo in August for the commercialization of Vanflyta (quizartinib) in China. Using these platforms, QureBio has built a robust pipeline of drug candidates aimed at previously intractable diseases. QureBio’s lead candidate, Q-1802, is a claudin18.2/PD-L1 bispecific antibody for the treatment of solid tumors that received regulatory clearance to initiate clinical trials in both China and the U.S. in March 2021. The company said in January 2026 that it would present positive phase 2 results for Q-1802 at ASCO, and that a phase 3 trial for the asset had already been approved in China. The company has successfully launched several innovative products in China, including Enzeshu, COSELA, Enweida, Endostar, and Enlituo. Biotech in China: A thriving industry China’s biotech industry has undergone a momentous shift in recent decades, evolving from a generics-focused space to a thriving biotech ecosystem . This is largely thanks to the fact that, back in 2015, the Chinese government ushered in a slate of reforms that have since enabled the biopharma industry to thrive. One of the main changes in the country included regulators beginning to pilot the Marketing Authorization Holder system, which allows drug developers to use contract manufacturers instead of having to build costly in-house production or sell intellectual property to large firms. Furthermore, generic drugs were required to show bioequivalence to their reference branded products to improve the overall quality in this area, and China’s FDA started to allow foreign clinical data to support applications. Consequently, China’s biotechnology sector is now experiencing explosive growth, transitioning from a manufacturing base to a global hub for innovation in areas like biopharmaceuticals and genetic engineering . Fueled by government support, increased investment, and an influx of talent, Chinese companies are developing novel drugs and creating global partnerships, presenting a significant challenge to established Western biotech industries. In fact, certain reports suggest that China has pulled ahead of the U.S. in key areas of the life sciences, and the U.S. may only have a handful of years to regain dominance in the sector. Meanwhile, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and biomaterials is further driving innovation and expanding the market’s potential. Table of contents Abogen Biosciences Technology: mRNA therapies Disease areas: Oncology, immunology, and infectious diseases Recent news: Initiated phase 3 trial of shingles vaccine candidate ABO1108 Abogen Biosciences makes it onto this list by virtue of an impressive $700 million series C round that it bagged in August 2021 – still one of the biggest ever private biotech funding rounds. This was swiftly followed by another $300 million investment round in November 2021. Abogen is one of the few Chinese biotech companies that has self-developed all its key messenger RNA (mRNA) platform technologies, across mRNA synthesis, delivery, and manufacturing. Its mission is ultimately to develop therapies derived from mRNA technology , including immunotherapies for cancer, protein replacement therapies, and vaccines for infectious diseases, including a vaccine against COVID-19, which was granted emergency use authorization (EUA) in Indonesia in 2022, making it the first China-made mRNA vaccine authorized for use anywhere in the world. The mRNA company’s lead candidate is ABO2011, which is currently being tested in a phase 1/2 trial as a monotherapy or in combination with the monoclonal antibody drug toripalimab in patients with advanced solid tumors. Another of its main candidates, a shingles vaccine dubbed ABO1108, which trains the immune system to fight the varicella-zoster virus, entered into a phase 3 trial in June 2026. Also part of Abogen’s portfolio is a novel KRAS mRNA cancer vaccine, ABO2102, in both China and the U.S. According to the company, the candidate is China’s first therapeutic cancer vaccine targeting multiple – in this case five – KRAS mutations. Meanwhile, in December 2025, Simcere also forged an exclusive licensing agreement with Ipsen for the French biopharma to obtain global rights outside of Greater China for SIM0613, an ADC with best-in-class potential. Targeting the LRRC15 protein, the asset is designed for enhanced tumor penetration and differentiated anti-tumor activity in solid tumors with the highest unmet needs. And, most recently, Simcere entered into an exclusive license agreement with Roche at the start of this month for the development and commercialization of SIM0660, a trispecific antibody targeting CD79a, CD19, and CD3. With its potential dual-targeting approach to CD79a and CD19, the candidate is designed to provide broad coverage across B-cell-mediated diseases and may offer a differentiated therapeutic approach for patients previously treated with CD20- or CD19-directed therapies. It also has therapeutic potential for B-cell-mediated autoimmune diseases, where targeted depletion of pathogenic B cells may provide clinical benefit. VelaVigo Technology: Multispecific antibodies and ADCs Disease areas: Oncology, immunology, neurology, and ophthalmology Recent news: Successfully closed over $60 million in pre-A+ funding With a highly efficient discovery engine and strong capabilities in translational medicine, Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC), and early clinical development, Chinese biotech company VelaVigo is focused on the discovery and development of multispecific antibodies and ADCs for cancer, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, neurodegenerative disorders, and eye diseases. Since its inception in 2021, the company has built a pipeline of more than ten multi-specific antibodies and ADC molecules for oncology and autoimmune diseases, and has also set up VelaVigo Bio, Inc. in the U.S. to drive clinical development and partnerships globally. In April 2025, the company announced its second out-licensing agreement for a first-in-class candidate to Ollin Biosciences, granting Ollin an exclusive license to develop, manufacture, and commercialize its bispecific antibody, VBS-102, globally (excluding Greater China). This agreement followed VelaVigo’s first licensing deal with Avenzo Therapeutics in November 2024 and the successful close of a $50 million pre-A funding round in February 2025. Meanwhile, not long after, in July 2025, the company announced the successful closing of over $60 million in pre-A+ funding. Biotech in China: A thriving industry China’s biotech industry has undergone a momentous shift in recent decades, evolving from a generics-focused space to a thriving biotech ecosystem . This is largely thanks to the fact that, back in 2015, the Chinese government ushered in a slate of reforms that have since enabled the biopharma industry to thrive. One of the main changes in the country included regulators beginning to pilot the Marketing Authorization Holder system, which allows drug developers to use contract manufacturers instead of having to build costly in-house production or sell intellectual property to large firms. Furthermore, generic drugs were required to show bioequivalence to their reference branded products to improve the overall quality in this area, and China’s FDA started to allow foreign clinical data to support applications. Consequently, China’s biotechnology sector is now experiencing explosive growth, transitioning from a manufacturing base to a global hub for innovation in areas like biopharmaceuticals and genetic engineering . Fueled by government support, increased investment, and an influx of talent, Chinese companies are developing novel drugs and creating global partnerships, presenting a significant challenge to established Western biotech industries. In fact, certain reports suggest that China has pulled ahead of the U.S. in key areas of the life sciences, and the U.S. may only have a handful of years to regain dominance in the sector. Meanwhile, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and biomaterials is further driving innovation and expanding the market’s potential. 15 biotech companies in China you should know about
Photo credits: Hanson Lu Add Labiotech as your Google Preferred Source Newsletter Signup - Under Article / In Page " * " indicates required fields China’s biotech scene has evolved significantly over the last few years, with companies increasingly developing novel drugs and attracting international attention through partnerships and out-licensing deals. Earlier this week, the country set out its latest five-year plan for its pharma industry, with an aim of being responsible for at least 25% of first-in-class drugs on the global market in order to cement its emerging status as a hotbed for innovative research and development (R&D). In this article, we look at 15 Chinese companies that are currently contributing to the country’s thriving biotech industry. Table of contents Abogen Biosciences Technology: mRNA therapies Disease areas: Oncology, immunology, and infectious diseases Recent news: Initiated phase 3 trial of shingles vaccine candidate ABO1108 Abogen Biosciences makes it onto this list by virtue of an impressive $700 million series C round that it bagged in August 2021 – still one of the biggest ever private biotech funding rounds. This was swiftly followed by another $300 million investment round in November 2021. Abogen is one of the few Chinese biotech companies that has self-developed all its key messenger RNA (mRNA) platform technologies, across mRNA synthesis, delivery, and manufacturing. Its mission is ultimately to develop therapies derived from mRNA technology , including immunotherapies for cancer, protein replacement therapies, and vaccines for infectious diseases, including a vaccine against COVID-19, which was granted emergency use authorization (EUA) in Indonesia in 2022, making it the first China-made mRNA vaccine authorized for use anywhere in the world. The mRNA company’s lead candidate is ABO2011, which is currently being tested in a phase 1/2 trial as a monotherapy or in combination with the monoclonal antibody drug toripalimab in patients with advanced solid tumors. Another of its main candidates, a shingles vaccine dubbed ABO1108, which trains the immune system to fight the varicella-zoster virus, entered into a phase 3 trial in June 2026. Also part of Abogen’s portfolio is a novel KRAS mRNA cancer vaccine, ABO2102, in both China and the U.S. According to the company, the candidate is China’s first therapeutic cancer vaccine targeting multiple – in this case five – KRAS mutations. Antengene Technology: T cell engagers and antibody therapies Disease areas: Oncology and immunology Recent news:  Entered into a partnership with K2 Therapeutics for ATG-106 Antengene is focused primarily on developing therapies for oncology and immunology indications. The Chinese biotech company’s pipeline spans from preclinical to commercial, with key investigational candidates including the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) ATG-022, the oral CD73 inhibitor ATG-037, the bispecific antibody ATG-101, the bispecific ADC ATG-125, the bifunctional fusion protein ATG-207, as well as T cell engager programs developed using Antengene’s proprietary AnTenGager platform. The first patient was dosed in a phase 3 trial of ATG-022 earlier this week. To date, Antengene has obtained 33 investigational new drug approvals in the U.S. and Asia, and obtained new drug application approvals in 10 Asia-Pacific markets. Its lead commercial asset, XPOVIO (selinexor), is approved in mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, South Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Australia, and has been included in the national insurance schemes in five of these markets.
